In the dappled, sullen green light of a wide river, a predator slides through the tall water grass on the hunt. Its long sleek body 
swimming silently, its peculiar crescent-shaped pupils seeking movement in the vertical kelp forest, as well as discerning any variation 
in color that breaks through the deep greenery. Th roughout the sullen day the larkiera patrol the long rivers that stretch through the 
Wealdwoods, the dark of the canopy above suiting their stalking behavior. Th ough an effective hunter with its trap-like teeth and agile 
maneuverability, the larkiera is far from the top of the Fenland’s trophic food-chain, and so it protects itself with a quickly lashing tail 
and dozens of dorsal spines that deter larger threats from immediately attacking it.

Encountering Th e larkiera pays little heed to anything beyond 
what it can sink its teeth into. In the murky waters of its domain, 
a flash of color can catch its eye within the river grasses and lure 
it to be caught, though the smell of blood in the water will ward 
off this predatory fi sh. Unlike many creatures in the rivers, the 
larkiera is solely a hunter, and not a scavenger.
